title: Karpov against Kasparov, 1985: the last game, and where it turned
outcomes: Tries each of five key moments before seeing the move and compares the attempt with the engine's first choice
Says where in the game the engine's rating turned, and what that does and does not show
Names the two questions the lesson asks at each moment: which pawn break is available, and what the other side wants to play

steps.text: **Karpov (White) against Kasparov (Black)**, game 24, Moscow, 9 November 1985: the last game of their world championship match, a Sicilian Defense. Kasparov won it and became world champion (Wikipedia, chessgames). You will play five moments, four as Black and one as White, then compare with the engine's first choice and with the game. Engine ratings are evidence at a stated depth, not proof.

steps.caption: Moves 1 to 23. Step through them; the first decision comes at the end.

line.say: The pawn goes to f4.
The g-pawn advances to g4.
The pawn advances again, to g5.
Black's knight goes to b4, next to the pawn on c2.
Bishop to e3. Black to move: your first decision is next.

steps.caption: Moves 23 to 26. Both sides regroup here: the black rooks change files, and the white king and a rook step back.

line.say: Re7: the rook moves to the seventh rank.
The second rook goes to e8.
Black plays the pawn break ...f5.
Black recaptures on f6 with the knight.

claims.statement: The first move of the line is legal.

steps.text: **What to check before you decide.** Two ideas from earlier lessons are at work in the next moves: a pawn break that opens a file for your pieces, and the question of what the other side wants to play. Ask both before each move. These are questions, not rules of thumb with guarantees: the engine, not the idea, decides whether a break is good in a given position.

steps.caption: Moves 31 to 33. White captures the pawn on g5 and Black's knight lands on g4.

line.say: Black plays the break ...g5.
White takes the pawn on g5.
The knight jumps to g4.
The queen goes to d2. Black to move.

claims.statement: The first move of the line is legal.

steps.caption: 33...Nxe3 and White's recapture. Black to move again.

line.say: The knight takes the bishop on e3.
The queen takes back. Black to move: next decision.

claims.statement: The first move of the line is legal.

line.say: The knight takes the pawn on c2.
The white queen goes to b6.
The bishop goes to a8. White to move: the last decision.

claims.statement: The first move of the line is legal.

steps.caption: The position after 36.Rxd6, Black to move. At depth 16 the engine rates it between 1.5 and 4 pawns in Black's favour.

line.say: The rook goes to b7.
Black's rook takes the knight on b3.
The rook takes the pawn on b2.
White's king steps to h1.
The bishop takes on g2 with check.
The king takes the bishop. My two sources disagree on the moves that follow, so the line stops here.

claims.statement: At depth 16 the position after 36.Rxd6 is rated 1.5 to 4 pawns in Black's favour (White's point of view).

steps.text: **What this game used.** The skills behind it are *Prophylaxis*, *Pawn breaks and levers* and *Defence by waiting*; the last decision is *Comparing resulting positions*. At depth 16 the engine rated the position about level before 36.Rxd6 and clearly in Black's favour after it, so that is where the rating turned. The earlier decisions were smaller steps. Go back to those lessons to learn the skills themselves.

steps.prompt: Which of the five moments (23...Re7, 31...g5, 33...Nxe3, 34...Nxc2, 36.Qxb8) would you have missed in a game of your own, and what would you have had to notice to find it?

Colour, date and remarks on the game: ChessBase newsroom and thechesspedia.net pages (read; partial, no full score) [S]. Not used in the lesson text beyond the result

No annotator's commentary was copied; all wording is ours. Course design: docs/course-families.md
